I’m 53 years old and I’ve farmed these 8 mu in Liuzhuang, Quzhou County, for more than thirty years. I finished senior high school, so unlike some of the older men in the village I can read the nutrient charts on the fertilizer bags and work out my own rates, but I’m still not one to gamble the family’s income on fancy experiments. The wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage, and now that it’s greening up in early March I’m looking at the whole year ahead. I’ll stick with the winter wheat–summer maize double crop. It’s tight, but it’s what this land and this climate are built for.

Last year my wheat made 510 kg/mu and the maize 560 kg/mu. This year I’m aiming for 520 kg/mu on the wheat and 580 kg/mu on the maize. I’m keeping the same improved wheat variety that’s been reliable, but for the maize I’m switching to the hybrid that Old Wang down the road planted last year—he got nearly 600 kg/mu and the grain buyer paid a good price for it. For fertilizer, I figure 18 kg of nitrogen per mu on the wheat: 10 kg went down as base dressing last autumn, and I’ll topdress another 8 kg at jointing. I’ll also apply 6 kg phosphorus and 6 kg potassium per mu. For the maize I plan 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, half at planting and half at the big trumpet stage. I know the extension office says 15 kg N is enough, but I’ve seen what happens when you cut it too fine—the leaves yellow and you lose 100 kg. I’d rather waste a little money than risk a bad year.

Water is what keeps me up at night. The electricity for the tube-well pump gets more expensive every season, so I have to count every irrigation. I’ll water the wheat three times: once at green-up now, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. For the maize, twice should do it if the summer rains don’t fail—once at jointing and once at filling. For chemicals, I’ll spray the wheat twice: a herbicide in early spring and a fungicide at heading to keep powdery mildew off. For the maize I’ll do two sprays as well, a pre-emergence herbicide and one insecticide when the armyworms show up, which they always do around here. Tillage is the biggest time constraint. The wheat ground was already rotary tilled before sowing. For the maize, there’s no time to plough after wheat harvest in mid-June—I’ll use no-tillage direct seeding. Every day counts; if I miss that early summer heat window, the yield drops fast.
